questions.q: Historically, what did ZooKeeper actually do for a Kafka cluster?
options: Handled all producer serialization automatically
Replaced the need for partitions entirely
Stored cluster metadata, elected the controller broker, and detected broker failures via session timeouts
Served as Kafka's primary message storage engine
questions.explain: ZooKeeper was Kafka's external coordination layer for cluster-wide metadata and controller election, not a data storage engine.

questions.q: What operational cost did running ZooKeeper alongside Kafka impose, per this lesson?
options: It doubled the number of partitions required per topic
It had no operational cost at all, only a licensing cost
It required every consumer to also run its own ZooKeeper instance
Every cluster was really two systems to run, patch, monitor, and scale — the Kafka brokers and a separate ZooKeeper ensemble
questions.explain: ZooKeeper was a fully separate system with its own failure modes and operational surface area, on top of the Kafka brokers themselves.

questions.q: How does KRaft replace ZooKeeper's function, according to this lesson?
options: KRaft delegates controller election to the consumer groups themselves
KRaft removes the need for any cluster metadata to be tracked at all
KRaft is simply a newer, faster version of ZooKeeper installed alongside Kafka
A quorum of Kafka's own controller nodes use the Raft algorithm to agree on cluster metadata directly, with no external system
questions.explain: KRaft builds consensus directly into Kafka's own controller nodes, eliminating the need for a separate coordination system.

questions.q: As of Kafka 4.0, what is the status of ZooKeeper mode, per this lesson?
options: ZooKeeper is required for any cluster larger than three brokers
ZooKeeper became the new recommended default, replacing KRaft
ZooKeeper and KRaft are both equally supported with no preference either way
ZooKeeper support was removed entirely — KRaft is the only supported mode
questions.explain: KRaft became production-ready starting with Kafka 3.3, and Kafka 4.0 removed ZooKeeper support entirely.

questions.q: What kind of information does the controller (ZooKeeper- or KRaft-based) actually need to track, per this lesson's tie-back to Lesson 11?
options: Only the contents of consumer offsets, nothing about brokers
Facts like who's the leader, who's in the ISR, and whether a broker is alive — durable, cluster-wide agreed-upon truth
The controller has no relationship to leader election at all
Only which serialization format each topic uses
questions.explain: The controller's job is exactly the metadata Lesson 11's leader-failover sequence depends on being tracked reliably.
